questions.q: According to Anthropic's own guidance on building agents, what does an agent's autonomy bring along with its usefulness?
options: The potential for compounding errors, since one wrong step can become the basis for the next
A guarantee that every action will be correct
The complete removal of any need for testing
A reduction in API token usage
questions.explain: Anthropic's guidance notes that autonomy helps agents scale tasks in trusted environments, but comes with higher costs and "the potential for compounding errors" — an uncaught mistake becomes the foundation for the next decision.

questions.q: Where does the natural pause point for a human-approval checkpoint already exist in the tool-calling round trip?
options: There is no such point; approval has to be bolted on outside the API entirely
Only inside the system prompt, before any API call is made
In the gap between receiving a tool_use block (stop_reason: "tool_use") and sending back a tool_result — nothing requires executing immediately
Only after the final text response has already been shown to the user
questions.explain: When Claude calls a tool, the API returns stop_reason "tool_use" and a tool_use block, then stops. Your application code decides what happens next, so holding that gap open for a human is a natural, not bolted-on, checkpoint.

questions.q: Which of these three signals, from this lesson's rule of thumb, suggests a tool call should require human approval?
options: The action is read-only and has no side effects
The action is irreversible, costly, or the agent's own result looks low-confidence
The action is one the agent has already performed successfully many times before
The action only affects a draft that hasn't been sent anywhere yet
questions.explain: The lesson's rule of thumb flags irreversible actions (can't be undone), costly ones (real money, risk, or reputation), and low-confidence ones (the agent itself seems uncertain) as the ones that warrant a human checkpoint.

questions.q: Why would gating every single tool call behind human approval, including simple read-only lookups, be the wrong design choice?
options: It would violate the Claude API's terms of service
It is technically impossible to approve a read-only call
It slows the agent down for no safety benefit, since a lookup has no irreversible or costly consequence to guard against
Read-only calls are not supported by the tool_use mechanism
questions.explain: A read-only lookup can't cause the kind of irreversible or costly harm a checkpoint exists to prevent, so gating it only adds latency without reducing any real risk.

questions.q: What is meant by a "compounding error" in an agent's multi-step loop?
options: An error that only ever affects the final output, never intermediate steps
A mistake the agent doesn't catch, which it then treats as true and builds its next decision on top of
An error caused exclusively by a network timeout
A bug that only occurs when two agents run at the same time
questions.explain: Because an agent observes its own prior results to decide its next action, an uncaught mistake doesn't stay isolated — the agent treats it as ground truth and takes a further action on top of it, compounding the problem.
